## Proposition 12.16
**Statement:** Given two circles about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater circle an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the greater and EFGH the lesser of the two given circles, and let K be their common centre. Through K draw a straight line and produce it in both directions until it meets the circumference of the greater circle at B and D (P1, P2). Then BD is a diameter of the greater circle (D1.17), and KB, KD, being drawn from the centre to the circumference, are equal (D1.15).

**Step 2.** Let KD meet the circumference of the lesser circle at G. Since EFGH is the lesser circle, its radius KG is less than the radius KD of the greater circle (D3.1); hence G falls between K and D, and KG is a part of KD (CN5).

**Step 3.** From G draw GA at right angles to BD (1.11), and produce it in both directions until it meets the circumference of the greater circle at A and C (P2), G lying between A and C. Then AC is a straight line in the greater circle, and since the angles which AC makes with BD at G are right, KG is the perpendicular drawn from the centre K to AC. Let BAD be the arc of the greater circle cut off by the diameter BD on the side of A; by D1.17 the diameter bisects the circle, so the arc BAD is the half of the whole circumference.

**Step 4.** The arc AD is a part of the arc BAD; therefore the arc BAD is greater than the arc AD (CN5). Bisect the arc BAD (3.30); bisect that half of it which ends at D; bisect again that half of the last arc which ends at D; and continue in this way. At every bisection the arc ending at D is halved; hence, the arc BAD and the arc AD being two unequal magnitudes, by 10.1 (whose argument holds equally when exactly the half is taken away each time) there will at length be left an arc ending at D which is less than the arc AD. Let LD be this arc, so that arc LD is less than arc AD.

**Step 5.** The point L lies on the arc AD. For L is a point of the arc BAD; and if L lay on the arc BA, or coincided with A, then the arc AD would be a part of the arc LD, or equal to it, so that the arc LD would not be less than the arc AD (CN5), contrary to Step 4. Hence L lies between A and D on the arc AD.

**Step 6.** The arc BAD is double of its half, that half is double of its own half, and so on down to the arc LD; hence the arc BAD is measured by the arc LD, that is, it is a multiple of the arc LD (D5.2). Let the arc BAD be m times the arc LD. And the whole circumference of the greater circle is double of the arc BAD (Step 3, D1.17); therefore the whole circumference is 2m times the arc LD.

**Step 7.** Join KA, KL, KC (P1). Since L lies on the arc AD (Step 5), the radius KL falls within the angle AKD, so that the angle LKD is a part of the angle AKD; therefore the angle LKD is less than the angle AKD (CN5). Again, since G, a point of the straight line KD, lies on AC between A and C, the straight line KD falls within the angle AKC, so that the angle AKD is a part of the angle AKC; therefore the angle AKD is less than the angle AKC (CN5). Consequently the angle LKD is less than the angle AKC.

**Step 8.** In the triangles LKD, AKC the two sides KL, KD are equal to the two sides KA, KC respectively, all of them being drawn from the centre K to the circumference of the greater circle (D1.15); and the angle LKD contained by KL, KD is less than the angle AKC contained by KA, KC (Step 7). Therefore the base LD is less than the base AC (1.24).

**Step 9.** From K draw KO perpendicular to LD (1.12). Then KO and KG are the perpendiculars drawn from the centre to the straight lines LD and AC in the greater circle (Step 3). If KO were less than KG, then LD would be nearer to the centre than AC (D3.5), and so LD would be greater than AC (3.15); and if KO were equal to KG, then LD and AC would be equally distant from the centre (D3.4), and so LD would be equal to AC (3.14). Each of these is impossible by Step 8. Therefore KO is greater than KG.

**Step 10.** Since LD is itself a straight line in the greater circle, it is not greater than the diameter (3.15). Beginning at D, fit into the greater circle a straight line DP1 equal to LD (4.1, D4.7); from P1 fit P1P2 equal to LD; and so on continually, each new straight line beginning where the preceding one ends and all proceeding in the same direction round the circumference. Each straight line so fitted, being equal to LD, cuts off from the greater circle an arc equal to the arc LD (3.28). Since the whole circumference is 2m times the arc LD (Step 6), when 2m such straight lines have been fitted the arcs cut off by them together make up the whole circumference, and the end P2m of the last of them coincides with D. Thus DP1P2...P(2m-1) is a polygon of 2m sides, and every angle of it lies on the circumference of the greater circle, since the extremities of each fitted straight line are on the circumference (D4.7); therefore the polygon is inscribed in the greater circle (D4.3).

**Step 11.** All the sides of the polygon are equal to LD, and therefore equal to one another (CN1); so the polygon is equilateral. And the number 2m of its sides is divisible into the two equal parts m and m; therefore it is an even number (D7.6).

**Step 12.** Each side of the polygon is a straight line in the greater circle equal to LD; therefore each side is equally distant from the centre with LD (3.14), that is, the perpendicular drawn from K to each side is equal to KO (D3.4), and hence is greater than KG (Step 9).

**Step 13.** Let S be any side of the polygon, and let KT be the perpendicular drawn from K to S (1.12), so that KT is equal to KO and greater than KG (Step 12). Let P be any point of S. If P coincides with T, then KP is KT, which is greater than KG. If P does not coincide with T, join KP (P1); in the triangle KTP the angle at T is right, so the angle KPT is less than a right angle (1.17), and therefore the side KP, which subtends the greater angle KTP, is greater than the side KT, which subtends the angle KPT (1.19); hence again KP is greater than KG. Thus every point P of the side S is at a distance from K greater than KG.

**Step 14.** Such a point P lies outside the lesser circle. For P is not on the circumference of the lesser circle, since otherwise KP would be equal to KG, both being drawn from the centre to that circumference (D1.15); and P is not within the lesser circle, since otherwise KP produced (P2) would meet its circumference at some point Q with KQ equal to KG (D1.15), and KP, being a part of KQ, would be less than KG (CN5). Hence no point of any side of the polygon lies on or within the lesser circle; no side meets the lesser circle at all, and therefore no side touches it (D3.2).

**Step 15.** Therefore in the greater circle ABCD there has been inscribed the equilateral polygon DP1P2...P(2m-1), having an even number of sides, which does not touch the lesser circle EFGH. Q.E.F.

heath_proof_text: Let ABCD, EFGH be the two given circles about the same centre K; thus it is required to inscribe in the greater circle ABCD an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the circle EFGH. For let the straight line BKD be drawn through the centre K, and from the point G let GA be drawn at right angles to the straight line BD and carried through to C; therefore AC touches the circle EFGH. [III. 16] Then, bisecting the circumference BAD, bisecting the half of it, and doing this continually, we shall leave a circumference less than AD. [X. 1] Let such be left, and let it be LD; from L let LM be drawn perpendicular to BD and carried through to N, and let LD, DN be joined; therefore LD is equal to DN. [III. 3, I. 4] Now, since LN is parallel to AC, and AC touches the circle EFGH, therefore LN does not touch the circle EFGH; therefore LD, DN are far from touching the circle EFGH. If then we fit into the circle ABCD straight lines equal to the straight line LD and placed continuously, there will be inscribed in the circle ABCD an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle EFGH.
